Wall Street is always looking for the next guru. But market history is filled with investors who scored big once, or even a few times, and then faded from history because they didn't keep hitting home runs. That's important to keep in mind as you consider the big shift toward electric stocks in Peter Thiel's portfolio.
Peter Thiel is a famous investor thanks to his successful investments in the technology sector, including Facebook (now called Meta (META +0.30%)). He also helped found PayPal (PYPL -0.49%) and Palantir (PLTR -0.68%). There's a good reason to listen to Thiel when it comes to investing, particularly in the technology sector.
Image source: Getty Images.
However, you don't want to forget that even good investors make mistakes. Warren Buffett, the longtime CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.41%)(BRKB +0.43%) was famous for pointing out his missteps even though his investment approach had been incredibly successful over the long term. Simply put, just because an investor is famous, it doesn't mean you should blindly follow them. They are human, just like you.
What Peter Thiel's shift into energy tells you is that you may want to consider following him... after you do your own homework. As your parents probably asked when you were a kid, "If your friend jumped off a cliff, would you jump too?" When it comes to investing, too many people follow without thinking. You don't want to be one of them.
Is energy the next big thing?
In this situation, Peter Thiel might be on to something. Electricity demand grew 10% between 2005 and 2025, but is expected to climb 60% between 2025 and 2045. That's a step change in demand driven by new technologies like artificial intelligence and electric vehicles. Thiel clearly knows a thing or two about technology and how the industry operates, so a deep dive into electric stocks is probably a good idea.
On that front, Thiel's purchases included independent power producers American Electric Power (AEP -0.15%) and Vistra (VST +0.19%). It also included utility CMS Energy (CMS +0.16%) and nuclear power start-up X-Energy (XE +3.08%). There's a lot going on in that mix, and it might be hard for investors with jobs and lives outside the stock market to dig into and understand all the companies Thiel has chosen to own.
How should you follow Thiel?
If you step back, however, Thiel's broad focus on electricity suggests you could pick just about any electricity-related stock for your portfolio. But you could also select a diversified exchange-traded fund (ETF), such as Vanguard Utilities ETF (VPU +0.43%), which would allow you to follow the electricity theme without taking on stock-specific risk. And if you don't have the time or energy to dig deeply into Thiel's specific stock picks, that may be the better way to play the power theme he appears to be leaning into.

PayPal expands stablecoin rails with custom token issuance platform
The PYUSDx stablecoin developer platform, backed by PayPal USD (PYUSD), is built with the help of M0 and MoonPay.
PYUSDx goes live with tokens issued by crypto native firms Saturn, Concrete and Cap.
The three go-live partners bring over $100 million of processed volume to the new platform.
Internet commerce giant PayPal PYPL$52.78·Market Closed extended its blockchain-based stablecoin effort to include a custom stablecoin developer platform, dubbed PYUSDx, built with the help of fiat-pegged token specialist M0 and crypto payments firm MoonPay, the companies said on Tuesday.
The platform, which gives any business the infrastructure to start a custom stablecoin backed by PayPal USD PYUSD$0.9996, was first teased back in February.
It’s now going live with tokens issued by crypto native firms Saturn, Concrete and Cap; which bring over $100 million of processed volume to the platform, according to a press release.
As the existing financial world comes onchain, competition is growing beyond the two major stablecoin issuers: Tether and Circle Internet (CRCL). Established payments companies are searching for a strategic advantage, particularly given the aggressive approach taken by payments giant Stripe, for instance.
PayPal, which CoinDesk revealed was the first payments institution to start offering crypto back in 2020, finds itself at a crossroads, where the sensible move is to partner with crypto specialists like M0 and Moonpay and double down on the tech.
PayPal has already been pushing hard with its PYUSD stablecoin, and the firm is in a unique position to bring this mainstream, considering the enormous reach of Venmo, said Luca Prosperi, CEO of M0, which also works with Stripe-owned Bridge and regulated custody firm Anchorage.
“As more financial institutions are getting involved, this creates fragmentation,” Prosperi said in an interview. “Plus, most of these financial institutions don’t really know how to engage with developers, so we abstract away the complexity and the risk and create a layer in the middle that facilitates integrations with all these new projects.”
PYUSDx tokens are issued by MoonPay Digital Assets Ltd. The platform combines M0’s universal stablecoin and digital token technology with MoonPay’s issuance and distribution infrastructure. Additional companies introducing stablecoins on PYUSDx include USD.AI and Fairblock, according to the release.

pages.title: PayPal Joins Meta's Muse AI Agent Alongside Stripe, Shopify
pages.text:
PayPal Customers Can Now Shop Through Meta’s Muse AI Agent
What Does PayPal Add to Meta’s Muse?
PayPal has joined Meta’s expanding payments network for Muse, giving users of the personal AI agent another way to complete purchases while extending PayPal’s merchant network into agent-driven shopping.
The integration allows PayPal customers to use Muse to shop and complete purchases at participating PayPal merchants. For Meta, the deal adds another established checkout option as it builds commerce directly into an AI agent that can search for products, interact with websites and act on a user’s instructions.
Muse launched on September 8 and differs from a conventional chatbot because it can perform tasks rather than simply provide answers. The agent can book travel, complete forms and make purchases, including continuing longer tasks in the background while requesting user approval before sensitive actions.
That ability already made payments a central part of Meta’s Muse launch. Adding PayPal now expands the number of merchants and payment credentials that can sit behind those agent-driven transactions.
How Does Muse Complete Purchases?
Meta launched Muse with Stripe’s Link wallet, allowing U.S. consumers to connect saved payment methods and authorize purchases through the agent. Link can complete checkout directly at more than one million businesses that support the service and can generate a single-use virtual card for approved purchases elsewhere.
PayPal gives Muse access to another large payment ecosystem rather than requiring the agent to rely on a single checkout infrastructure. Meta has also integrated Shopify’s Shop Pay and opened Muse to Shopify’s merchant catalog, creating multiple routes through which the agent can move from product discovery to payment.
The model is increasingly important because the competition in AI shopping is moving beyond which assistant can recommend the right product. The harder problem is whether that assistant can actually complete the transaction across enough merchants, payment methods and websites to become useful.
PayPal has already been building toward that model. Its earlier agreement to bring PayPal checkout into ChatGPT connected its merchant network to another AI shopping interface, showing that the company is pursuing distribution across multiple agent platforms rather than betting on one ecosystem.
The strategic value for PayPal is not simply another checkout integration. If consumers increasingly ask AI agents to find products and complete purchases, payment companies will compete to become the infrastructure those agents use automatically. Merchant reach, stored credentials and trusted authorization could become more important than owning the shopping interface itself.
Why Is PayPal Preparing Merchants for AI Agents?
The Muse deal follows PayPal’s September support for WebMCP, an emerging standard designed to make existing merchant websites easier for AI assistants to understand and interact with.
For participating PayPal merchants, WebMCP can expose structured information about products, inventory, carts and checkout to compatible agents without requiring merchants to build a separate AI storefront. The consumer can still approve the payment through PayPal while the agent handles more of the discovery and navigation process.
That matters if agentic commerce develops through the existing web rather than through a handful of closed AI marketplaces. PayPal can potentially make merchants already using its infrastructure accessible to new AI shopping interfaces without forcing those businesses to rebuild their checkout systems.
The payments industry is moving in the same direction. Visa has been developing infrastructure for AI agents to initiate transactions under predefined controls, while a live European test involving Worldline, ING and Visa has already shown that agent-driven purchases can operate within existing banking and authentication rules.
Who Controls the Checkout in Agentic Commerce?
The emerging competition is creating several layers. Meta, OpenAI and other AI companies can control the consumer interface. Shopify and other commerce platforms can provide merchant catalogs. PayPal, Stripe and card networks can provide payment credentials, authorization and settlement.
RelatedPayPal Q2 2026: $1.38 EPS Beat, But Operating Income Fell 8%
No single company necessarily needs to control every layer. For PayPal, that could be an advantage. Its business can benefit whenever an agent sends a customer to a PayPal-supported merchant or uses PayPal to complete the transaction, even if another company owns the AI assistant itself.
The challenge is that the same logic attracts competitors. Stripe’s Link already gives Muse broad checkout coverage, while Shop Pay creates another direct route into Shopify stores. Amazon has taken a different approach by blocking Muse from shopping on its platform, showing that merchant access cannot be assumed.
That makes coverage the immediate battleground. An AI shopping agent becomes more useful as the number of websites, catalogs and payment systems it can transact with increases. By adding PayPal, Meta is expanding that reach, while PayPal is making sure its merchant network remains part of the transaction if shopping begins moving from browser tabs to AI agents.

PayPal (PYPL) Stock Jumps 5% on Takeover Buzz and Meta Deal Chatter
PayPal (PYPL) stock jumped 5% on takeover rumors and a Meta buyout pitch, while Deutsche Bank raised its price target to $55.
By Trader EdgeSeptember 26, 20263 Mins Read
PayPal (PYPL) stock rose about 5% on Friday to $55.13.
Traders cited a Betaville “uncooked” alert pointing to a possible all-stock takeover bid from a West Coast tech company.
PayPal’s board reportedly wants an all-cash deal, not stock.
The Stripe-Advent consortium walked away last month after a dispute over a $2 billion break fee, ending a bid worth over $50 billion.
Deutsche Bank raised its price target on PYPL to $55 from $50, keeping a Hold rating.
PayPal (PYPL) stock climbed roughly 5% on Friday, trading at $55.13 as takeover chatter swirled around the fintech company.
Traders pointed to a Betaville “uncooked” alert circulating Friday morning. The alert suggested a U.S. technology company based on the West Coast could be weighing an all-stock takeover of PayPal.
That’s a different structure than what PayPal’s board reportedly wants. Sources say the board prefers an all-cash transaction over a stock swap.
This isn’t the first takeover talk PayPal has faced this year. Stripe and private equity firm Advent had been in discussions to buy the company outright.
Those talks reportedly hit a snag over a $2 billion break fee. If the deal collapsed, someone would have owed that fee, and neither side could agree on terms.
The Stripe-Advent consortium had considered paying up to $68 per share in cash. That would have valued PayPal at more than $50 billion.
Last month, the consortium reportedly abandoned the pursuit entirely. PayPal has been searching for a suitor since.
PayPal did not respond to requests for comment on the latest speculation, according to Benzinga.
Separately, Great Hill Capital Chairman Thomas Hayes floated his own idea this week. He suggested Meta Platforms (META) should be the one to buy PayPal.
Hayes pitched a price tag of $90 billion. He said that works out to roughly a 7% free-cash-flow yield, calling it accretive whether Meta paid in cash, stock, or some mix of both.
His reasoning centers on data. Hayes argued that pairing PayPal’s transaction data with Meta’s ad business could build advertising capabilities on par with Amazon (AMZN).
He estimated a three-to-four-year payback window on that $90 billion price. Hayes framed the idea as him thinking out loud as a shareholder, not as insider knowledge of any deal.
PYPL is trading about 3% above its 20-day moving average of $53.45. It’s still about 3% below its 50-day average of $56.79, putting the stock in what chart watchers call a decision zone.
The longer-term picture looks steadier. Shares sit roughly 8% above the 100-day average and 9% above the 200-day average.
Relative strength index (RSI) reads 50.75. That’s neutral, not overbought or oversold.
The moving averages tell a mixed story. The 20-day average is still below the 50-day average, a bearish short-term signal.
But the 50-day average remains above the 200-day average following August’s golden cross. That’s typically viewed as a longer-term bullish setup.
Traders are watching whether PYPL can reclaim the 50-day level and hold it. Doing so would turn Friday’s bounce into something more durable.
Key resistance sits at $59.50, a ceiling tied to a recent stall zone. Key support sits at $52, near where the 20-day and 200-day averages converge.
Separately, Deutsche Bank raised its price target on PayPal to $55 from $50 on Friday. The bank kept its Hold rating unchanged.
PayPal shares were up 4.80% to $55.13 at the time of publication Friday.

The payments industry is full of lucrative businesses. Just look at Visa, Mastercard, and American Express. But relative newcomer PayPal (PYPL -0.49%) has struggled mightily in recent years, despite past success. And its investor base has paid the price.
This fintech stock trades at a gut-wrenching 83% off its record high of $305.13 (as of Sept. 29), set in July 2021. Are shares too cheap to ignore right now? Prospective investors will understand that there's only one thing that would send the stock price back to its previous all-time high.
Image source: PayPal.
Branded checkout needs to thrive once again
From the second quarter of 2021 to the most recent quarter (Q2 2026 ended June 30), PayPal's total payment volume (TPV) rose 56%. This helped drive revenue 40% higher during that time. What's more, the company's free cash flow grew by 64%.
While not Earth-shattering growth rates, these are still encouraging financial trends. But despite the fundamental momentum, PayPal's shares have wildly disappointed investors.
I think the culprit is the company's branded checkout solution, which displays the PayPal button for consumers to use when making purchases. This is the company's crown jewel segment, as it's been the most lucrative in the past. In the first and second quarters, TPV here was up just 2%.
This might signal that the PayPal brand is losing its sway among merchants and consumers. Competitive forces are intense these days. Apple Pay is perhaps the most obvious threat, leveraging its advantage of being embedded in the most popular hardware devices.
Furthermore, PayPal's weakness in branded checkout could suggest that its user base is more economically sensitive. Because the platform leans toward discretionary spending activity, the current macroeconomic backdrop could be a headwind as these consumers pull back.

How patient are you willing to be?
For the stock to have a chance at reclaiming its record high, the branded checkout solution has to start picking up steam. This isn't guaranteed, of course. And given trends over recent years, investors are losing confidence.
But if you're still bullish on the business, the cheap price-to-earnings ratio of 10.2 makes this a value stock candidate. And for what it's worth, PayPal remains firmly profitable. It's using FCF to repurchase shares aggressively. This could provide a floor for the stock price, although investor patience will be tested. Shares have been beaten down for a while.
PayPal investors could earn a quick profit if a suitor acquires the business. In July, PayPal rejected a $53 billion takeover bid (priced at $60.50 per share, still well below the all-time record) from Stripe and Advent International, so the board certainly signaled that it wants a much higher offer. Sound investing, however, isn't predicated on guessing when a takeover will happen.
This company has built a scaled global platform and pioneered digital payments for over two decades. But PayPal stock faces a challenging road ahead. I wouldn't bet on it rising 466% to get back to its peak price.

PayPal Survey Reveals Holiday Spending Isn't Slowing Down, But Shoppers Are Changing How They Spend
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 5:32 AM PDT 5 min read
As shoppers start earlier, seek more value and prioritize flexibility, PayPal offers more ways to help them make the most of their holiday budgets.
SAN JOSE, Calif., Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Holiday shoppers aren't necessarily spending less this year. They're changing how they spend. PayPal today released its 2026 Holiday Shopping Survey, revealing that nearly six in 10 Americans (58%) feel greater financial concern heading into the holidays, yet 64% still expect to spend the same or more than they did last holiday season. Faced with that tension, shoppers are planning earlier, setting budgets and looking for more ways to get value from every purchase.
Heading into the holidays, 58% of consumers feel greater financial concern, yet 64% still expect to spend the same or more than last year.
More than half (58%) plan to shop before Thanksgiving, while 67% are more likely to shop with a retailer that offers rewards or cash back. As consumers rethink how they manage holiday spending, PayPal offers more choice and flexibility through Pay Later options, rewarding ways to pay, and offers from top brands in the new PayPal app.
"What's changing isn't consumers' desire to spend during the holidays, but how they're going about it," said Frank Keller, President of Checkout Solutions & PayPal. "Shoppers are starting earlier and taking a more intentional approach, looking for deals, rewards and cash back to make every purchase count while still prioritizing the gifts and moments that matter most. As they look for ways to stretch their budgets, PayPal helps them turn that planning into action by bringing together offers, rewards and flexible payment options, including PayPal Pay Later, throughout the holiday season."
Consumers Are Taking Action to Make Holiday Budgets Go Further
With financial concerns top of mind, shoppers are taking practical steps to manage holiday spending and find value from every purchase, including:
Prioritizing budgets: Setting and sticking to a budget (36%) is the top way consumers plan to manage their holiday spending, followed by comparing prices (32%) and waiting for sales or promotions (31%).
Starting earlier: Two in five consumers plan to begin their holiday shopping by the end of October, and 29% plan to start shopping earlier than last year.
Maximizing rewards: More than two-thirds (67%) are willing to use all their saved rewards to help purchase the perfect gift, and 55% have saved rewards they could use for holiday shopping.
In addition to discovering deals from favorite brands in the PayPal app, shoppers can use the PayPal Cashback Mastercard®1 to earn 3% cash back on eligible purchases when they check out with PayPal.
Shoppers Are Making Tradeoffs to Preserve Gift-Giving
As holiday gift-giving remains a priority, consumers are making careful choices about where to cut back as they balance the season with financial pressures and rising costs.
Sacrifices are personal first: Consumers would cut back on dining out (39%) and gifts for themselves (35%) to make room for holiday spending.
Gift lists may be a little shorter: Twenty-nine percent would buy gifts for fewer people, while 34% would spend less on each individual gift.
Trading time for the perfect gift: Seventy percent are willing to visit multiple stores, while 63% would spend hours searching online for the perfect gift.
As shoppers plan their holiday gift list, clothing (52%), toys and games (38%), and beauty, personal care and fragrance (32%) are the top categories where they plan to buy this holiday season. For larger purchases or gifts for multiple people, flexible payment options from PayPal provide shoppers with another way to manage when and how they pay while keeping meaningful gift-giving within reach.
BNPL Has Become a Go-To Way to Manage Holiday Purchases
The survey also points to strong interest in flexible payment options such as Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL), as shoppers consider how to manage the timing and cost of planned holiday expenses. PayPal helps meet that need with Pay Later options including Pay in 42, which allows shoppers to split eligible purchases into four interest-free payments, and Pay Monthly3, which offers longer-term monthly payment plans. The survey found:
BNPL is a core part of the holiday payment mix: More than half of consumers (55%) have used or considered BNPL. Among those consumers, three-quarters plan to use or are considering using BNPL for holiday shopping.
Flexibility and control drive interest: Feeling more in control of their holiday budget and spreading the cost of purchases over time are each valued as BNPL benefits by 59% of consumers, while the flexibility to choose when and how to pay and the ability to take advantage of promotions are each valued by 60%.
BNPL can influence purchase decisions: Forty-two percent say they would be more likely to make a purchase if BNPL were available, 56% value BNPL's ability to help them manage the cost of a higher-value gift, and 57% say it would help them manage the cost of gifts for several people.
PayPal commissioned Morning Consult to survey a nationally representative sample of 2,005 U.S. adults from Sept. 2-4, 2026. The results have a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points.

What Could Derail PayPal Stock?
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 12:16 PM PDT 4 min read
PayPal (PYPL) stock has lost 24% in the twelve months to September 30, 2026, while the S&P 500 rose 14.4%. Investors are worried, and you need to know if that worry is overdone. PayPal needs its faster-growing businesses, such as Venmo, to earn more. PayPal also needs shoppers to keep choosing it at online checkout, where trouble could start. So what could go wrong for PayPal at online checkout?
PayPal could lose ground at checkout to competing ways to pay. The business at risk is online branded checkout, the PayPal button on a store's pay page. Management acknowledged the issue on the fiscal Q2 2026 call. Asked about markets outside the U.S., it said there is more competitive intensity across the landscape. Even so, management said PayPal's own performance improved slightly in Europe and was stable in the U.S.
So far, PayPal is holding its place. Online branded checkout volume grew 2% excluding currency moves, the same pace as the quarter before. That pace is slow next to PayPal as a whole. Total payment volume grew 9% in the same quarter, also excluding currency moves. So most of PayPal's volume growth is coming from outside branded checkout.
Is PayPal's Profit Growing As Fast As Its Payments?
No. Transaction margin is the profit PayPal makes on payments before its other operating costs. That profit grew 1% in fiscal Q2 2026, against 9% for payment volume excluding currency moves. Venmo and Braintree, two of PayPal's faster-growing businesses, grew volume in the mid-teens, yet PayPal's total profit on payments barely moved.
PayPal is also keeping a smaller cut of each payment. The take rate is the transaction revenue PayPal earns per dollar of payments. PayPal's take rate fell 7 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, to 1.61%. Management said the causes included co-marketing spending on branded checkout and faster growth at Venmo. So PayPal is already spending on marketing for its checkout button.
PayPal reports its whole business as one segment, so branded checkout has no revenue figure of its own. The company as a whole had revenue of $33.2 billion in fiscal 2025. Revenue grew 4.3% that year, down from 6.8% the year before.
The stock costs 9.4 times PayPal's yearly earnings, against 21.7 for the S&P 500. At that price, slow growth appears to be expected. Falling profit would be worse than slow growth, so holders of PayPal stock should watch for signs of it.
What Should You Watch In PayPal's Fiscal Q3 Report?
You should watch branded checkout growth and transaction margin growth in PayPal's fiscal Q3 2026 report. Checkout competition is a real threat to PayPal, but so far a slow one. Branded checkout is still growing, and management raised its full-year outlook for it to low single-digit volume growth.
Because PayPal reports its business as one segment, you cannot tell how much profit branded checkout brings in. So you cannot size the damage if checkout volume starts to shrink. The stock costs 9.4 times today's earnings. If those earnings fall, you are paying more for each dollar of profit than that number shows.
Management guided fiscal Q3 2026 transaction margin to slightly positive growth. PayPal's profit on payments would be shrinking if that number comes in negative. Management also called the holiday quarter always competitive.
PayPal is holding its place at checkout with 2% growth, but its profit on payments is barely growing. Transaction margin growth well above the guide would suggest PayPal's faster-growing businesses, such as Venmo and Braintree, are paying off. Branded checkout growth below 2% in the fiscal Q3 2026 report would be an early warning for PayPal stock.

Payments network operator PayPal (PYPL) saw its stock drop sharply after a consortium of buyout firm Advent International and payment processor Stripe walked away from a $53 billion (or $60.50 per share) bid after being rebuffed.
Now, PayPal has been embroiled in rumors of another takeover bid. Traders reported that an "uncooked" alert from Betaville suggested a U.S. technology company headquartered on the West Coast could be considering an all-stock acquisition of the fintech company. Reportedly, PayPal is looking for an all-cash offer. While nothing is confirmed, PayPal might not accept an offer that is not meaningfully above $70 per share, as Bernstein analysts estimate.

Agentic AI also offers a unique growth opportunity for a firm like PayPal, given its existing customer base.
While the takeover bid rumors are not yet conclusive, let's take a look at PayPal's current state.
PayPal Holdings runs a worldwide payments network that connects consumers and businesses across digital and physical channels. Its brands, including PayPal, Venmo, and Xoom, allow users to make purchases, transfer funds, receive payments, and access various financial services.
The company works with consumers, small businesses, global retailers, online marketplaces, and other corporate customers. In addition to processing payments, PayPal offers fraud management, payment authorization, and business analytics solutions designed to help merchants improve transactions and customer engagement. Headquartered in San Jose, California, the company has a market capitalization of approximately $46.43 billion.
PYPL stock has fallen 20% over the past 52 weeks, mainly because investors remain concerned about slowing growth, intense competition, and uncertainty over the company's turnaround. It reached a 52-week low of $38.46 in February but is up 39% from that level. However, the stock rose 24% over the past three months as investors saw signs of improvement. Reports of the potential takeover bid supported the stock by highlighting PayPal's strategic value.
On a forward-adjusted basis, PayPal's price-to-earnings (non-GAAP) ratio of 10.07x is lower than the industry average of 10.96x.
Revenue Growth in Q2 Raises Full-Year Profit Guidance
In the second quarter, PayPal reported 10% year-over-year (YoY) growth in total payment volume to $486.45 billion, while quarterly revenue rose 5% YoY to $8.68 billion. As operating cash flow improved sharply and capital spending remained modest, the company's free cash flow climbed 157% YoY to $1.78 billion. However, PayPal's adjusted operating margin dropped by 248 basis points to 17.4%. Adjusted EPS declined by 1% YoY to $1.38.
PayPal raised its fiscal 2026 non-GAAP EPS forecast to about $5.38, slightly above the $5.31 figure it recorded in fiscal 2025. In its last guidance, the company expected non-GAAP EPS to decline in the low single digits or increase slightly. For the current year, Wall Street analysts expect PayPal's EPS to increase by a modest 1.3% YoY to $5.38, followed by a 7.8% improvement to $5.80 in the next year. However, for the third quarter, EPS is projected to decrease 1.5% YoY to $1.32.
What Do Analysts Think About PYPL Stock?
In August, analysts at Piper Sandler raised the price target on PYPL stock from $42 to $59 while maintaining a "Neutral" rating, following reports that PayPal is negotiating a higher takeover bid from Stripe and Advent. The analyst saw this development as a potential strategic validation of the company's asset base. However, later reports suggested that the group is no longer pursuing the takeover after their initial offer was rebuffed. This led analysts at Truist Securities to lower PayPal's price target from $62 to $53 while keeping a "Hold" rating on its shares.
Contrarily, RBC Capital analysts raised PayPal's price target from $65 to $70 and maintained an "Outperform" rating as part of a broader research note on Fintech & Payments as RBC updates its valuation framework.
Wall Street analysts are taking a cautious stance on PYPL's stock now, with a consensus "Hold" rating overall. Of the 46 analysts rating the stock, four analysts gave a "Strong Buy" rating, and two analysts rated it "Moderate Buy," while a majority of 36 analysts are playing it safe with a "Hold" rating; one analyst suggested "Moderate Sell," and three analysts gave a "Strong Sell" rating. The consensus price target of $56.03 represents a 5% upside from current levels. The Street-high price target of $72 implies a 36% upside.

What Does PayPal Add to Meta’s Muse?
PayPal has joined Meta’s expanding payments network for Muse, giving users of the personal AI agent another way to complete purchases while extending PayPal’s merchant network into agent-driven shopping.
The integration allows PayPal customers to use Muse to shop and complete purchases at participating PayPal merchants. For Meta, the deal adds another established checkout option as it builds commerce directly into an AI agent that can search for products, interact with websites and act on a user’s instructions.
Muse launched on September 8 and differs from a conventional chatbot because it can perform tasks rather than simply provide answers. The agent can book travel, complete forms and make purchases, including continuing longer tasks in the background while requesting user approval before sensitive actions.
That ability already made payments a central part of Meta’s Muse launch. Adding PayPal now expands the number of merchants and payment credentials that can sit behind those agent-driven transactions.
How Does Muse Complete Purchases?
Meta launched Muse with Stripe’s Link wallet, allowing U.S. consumers to connect saved payment methods and authorize purchases through the agent. Link can complete checkout directly at more than one million businesses that support the service and can generate a single-use virtual card for approved purchases elsewhere.
PayPal gives Muse access to another large payment ecosystem rather than requiring the agent to rely on a single checkout infrastructure. Meta has also integrated Shopify’s Shop Pay and opened Muse to Shopify’s merchant catalog, creating multiple routes through which the agent can move from product discovery to payment.
The model is increasingly important because the competition in AI shopping is moving beyond which assistant can recommend the right product. The harder problem is whether that assistant can actually complete the transaction across enough merchants, payment methods and websites to become useful.
PayPal has already been building toward that model. Its earlier agreement to bring PayPal checkout into ChatGPT connected its merchant network to another AI shopping interface, showing that the company is pursuing distribution across multiple agent platforms rather than betting on one ecosystem.
The strategic value for PayPal is not simply another checkout integration. If consumers increasingly ask AI agents to find products and complete purchases, payment companies will compete to become the infrastructure those agents use automatically. Merchant reach, stored credentials and trusted authorization could become more important than owning the shopping interface itself.
Why Is PayPal Preparing Merchants for AI Agents?
The Muse deal follows PayPal’s September support for WebMCP, an emerging standard designed to make existing merchant websites easier for AI assistants to understand and interact with.
For participating PayPal merchants, WebMCP can expose structured information about products, inventory, carts and checkout to compatible agents without requiring merchants to build a separate AI storefront. The consumer can still approve the payment through PayPal while the agent handles more of the discovery and navigation process.
That matters if agentic commerce develops through the existing web rather than through a handful of closed AI marketplaces. PayPal can potentially make merchants already using its infrastructure accessible to new AI shopping interfaces without forcing those businesses to rebuild their checkout systems.
The payments industry is moving in the same direction. Visa has been developing infrastructure for AI agents to initiate transactions under predefined controls, while a live European test involving Worldline, ING and Visa has already shown that agent-driven purchases can operate within existing banking and authentication rules.
Who Controls the Checkout in Agentic Commerce?
The emerging competition is creating several layers. Meta, OpenAI and other AI companies can control the consumer interface. Shopify and other commerce platforms can provide merchant catalogs. PayPal, Stripe and card networks can provide payment credentials, authorization and settlement.

Amazon has taken a different approach by blocking Muse from shopping on its platform, showing that merchant access cannot be assumed.
That makes coverage the immediate battleground. An AI shopping agent becomes more useful as the number of websites, catalogs and payment systems it can transact with increases. PayPal (PYPL) stock climbed roughly 5% on Friday, trading at $55.13 as takeover chatter swirled around the fintech company.
Traders pointed to a Betaville “uncooked” alert circulating Friday morning. The alert suggested a U.S. technology company based on the West Coast could be weighing an all-stock takeover of PayPal.
That’s a different structure than what PayPal’s board reportedly wants. Sources say the board prefers an all-cash transaction over a stock swap.
This isn’t the first takeover talk PayPal has faced this year. Stripe and private equity firm Advent had been in discussions to buy the company outright.
Those talks reportedly hit a snag over a $2 billion break fee. If the deal collapsed, someone would have owed that fee, and neither side could agree on terms.
The Stripe-Advent consortium had considered paying up to $68 per share in cash. That would have valued PayPal at more than $50 billion.
Last month, the consortium reportedly abandoned the pursuit entirely. PayPal has been searching for a suitor since.
PayPal did not respond to requests for comment on the latest speculation, according to Benzinga.
Separately, Great Hill Capital Chairman Thomas Hayes floated his own idea this week. He suggested Meta Platforms (META) should be the one to buy PayPal.
Hayes pitched a price tag of $90 billion. He said that works out to roughly a 7% free-cash-flow yield, calling it accretive whether Meta paid in cash, stock, or some mix of both.
His reasoning centers on data. Hayes argued that pairing PayPal’s transaction data with Meta’s ad business could build advertising capabilities on par with Amazon (AMZN).
He estimated a three-to-four-year payback window on that $90 billion price. Hayes framed the idea as him thinking out loud as a shareholder, not as insider knowledge of any deal.
PYPL is trading about 3% above its 20-day moving average of $53.45. It’s still about 3% below its 50-day average of $56.79, putting the stock in what chart watchers call a decision zone.
The longer-term picture looks steadier. Shares sit roughly 8% above the 100-day average and 9% above the 200-day average.
Relative strength index (RSI) reads 50.75. That’s neutral, not overbought or oversold.
The moving averages tell a mixed story. The 20-day average is still below the 50-day average, a bearish short-term signal.
But the 50-day average remains above the 200-day average following August’s golden cross. That’s typically viewed as a longer-term bullish setup.
Traders are watching whether PYPL can reclaim the 50-day level and hold it. Doing so would turn Friday’s bounce into something more durable.
Key resistance sits at $59.50, a ceiling tied to a recent stall zone. Key support sits at $52, near where the 20-day and 200-day averages converge.
Separately, Deutsche Bank raised its price target on PayPal to $55 from $50 on Friday. The bank kept its Hold rating unchanged.
PayPal shares were up 4.80% to $55.13 at the time of publication Friday.

So what could go wrong for PayPal at online checkout?
PayPal could lose ground at checkout to competing ways to pay. The business at risk is online branded checkout, the PayPal button on a store's pay page. Management acknowledged the issue on the fiscal Q2 2026 call. Asked about markets outside the U.S., it said there is more competitive intensity across the landscape. Even so, management said PayPal's own performance improved slightly in Europe and was stable in the U.S.

Is PayPal's Profit Growing As Fast As Its Payments?
No. Transaction margin is the profit PayPal makes on payments before its other operating costs. That profit grew 1% in fiscal Q2 2026, against 9% for payment volume excluding currency moves. Venmo and Braintree, two of PayPal's faster-growing businesses, grew volume in the mid-teens, yet PayPal's total profit on payments barely moved.
PayPal is also keeping a smaller cut of each payment. The take rate is the transaction revenue PayPal earns per dollar of payments. PayPal's take rate fell 7 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, to 1.61%. Management said the causes included co-marketing spending on branded checkout and faster growth at Venmo. So PayPal is already spending on marketing for its checkout button.
PayPal reports its whole business as one segment, so branded checkout has no revenue figure of its own. The company as a whole had revenue of $33.2 billion in fiscal 2025. Revenue grew 4.3% that year, down from 6.8% the year before.
The stock costs 9.4 times PayPal's yearly earnings, against 21.7 for the S&P 500. At that price, slow growth appears to be expected. Falling profit would be worse than slow growth, so holders of PayPal stock should watch for signs of it.

Management guided fiscal Q3 2026 transaction margin to slightly positive growth. PayPal's profit on payments would be shrinking if that number comes in negative. Management also called the holiday quarter always competitive.
PayPal is holding its place at checkout with 2% growth, but its profit on payments is barely growing.
